pivot: Whether the safety/harm liability docket (product-liability or negligence theory against a frontier developer) produces a binding court ruling, or binding liability stays confined to the copyright/training-data track
pivot_observable: A federal court denies a motion to dismiss on a product-liability or negligence theory against a frontier AI developer (OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, Google, or xAI as developer, not merely a co-defendant)
pivot_because: If the safety docket binds, labs' deployment posture itself — staged release, red-teaming, duty of care toward users — becomes court-constrained, and the internal recursive-improvement work ai-rsi-timeline flags stops being invisible to any external check. If only copyright binds, courts reach data-sourcing and retraining schedules but leave the capability/safety axis genuinely unwatched, which is what lets ai-rsi-timeline's acceleration claim hold. That is a reorder of which activities are constrained, not a shift in confidence about one outcome. ai-pressure's candidate pivot (do model-destruction/retraining injunctions actually issue) only reorders within the data axis and leaves the safety axis's status unchanged either way, so it does not qualify.
rival_pivots_rejected: ai-pressure's implicit pivot (do plaintiffs win model-destruction/retraining injunctions over training corpora) only reorders outcomes within the copyright/data-sourcing axis — it doesn't touch whether the safety/harm docket is live, so both a yes and a no leave the RSI blind spot exactly where ai-rsi-timeline put it. lab-moves' pivot (which counterparty — regulator vs. insurer/contract vs. litigant — a lab cites publicly) is a matter of framing/attribution, not a different constraint regime; a lab citing discovery obligations and a lab citing contract terms both sit inside 'litigation exposure replaces statute,' the shared premise, and neither reorders the outcome set.
ruling: The case turns on whether courts extend binding liability from the training-data track into the safety/harm track by 2027-12-31; if they don't, internal recursive self-improvement research proceeds in a genuine observability gap that no installer in the brief is watching.
because: Two panelists put opposing answers to the same falsifiable on the record: ai-courts-decide's round-1/round-2 claim is that no such MTD denial occurs by 2027-12-31, while pressure-model's round-2 REVISE asserts the safety-posture axis is already anchored by a named, dated precedent (Garcia v. Character Technologies, M.D. Fla., May 2025) that denied a motion to dismiss on a duty-of-care theory against an AI developer. ai-courts-decide's visible round-2 DEFEND does not engage this citation in the truncated text available. Whichever way that specific fact resolves, it is the fact that decides whether the safety axis is court-constrained or court-blind, which is what every other minute's claim implicitly depends on.
threat_live: With no statute and (on the 'below' branch) courts confined to copyright, internal recursive self-improvement — agentic coding, automated ML R&D — has no external observer at all: no disclosure trigger, no capability threshold, no safety-docket ruling reaches it. This pairs with ai-pressure's point that cycle-1 voluntary safety-body commitments become litigation shields inside the copyright fight, which creates an incentive to keep those commitments cosmetic rather than substantive precisely where the RSI work is hardest to see.
strongest_minute: pressure-model — it revised in direct response to the record rather than restating, decomposed 'release/safety posture' into two separately-constrained components instead of treating it as one axis, and grounded its revision in a specific dated precedent rather than a general mechanism claim.
weakest_minute: ai-courts-decide — its round-2 DEFEND holds its falsifiable unchanged against a rival's specific counter-citation without visibly rebutting it, leaving the pivot's most important fact contested but unaddressed on its side of the record.
shared_assumption: All six minutes agree that litigation/contract/insurer exposure — not a regulator — becomes the binding channel once the statute is absent; none of them argues for this, they treat it as given. Within that, four (ai-pressure, lab-moves, ai-public-backlash, ai-courts-decide) implicitly equate 'no statute' with 'no regulator,' while pressure-model alone separates out export-control (BIS/ECRA) as a live, non-statutory regulatory installer — that distinction is argued, not assumed, and the other four's silence on it is a gap, not a rebuttal.
smuggled_assumption: ai-public-backlash's claim is conditional on 'a widely-publicized harm event (chatbot-related death, mass copyright verdict, or major security breach)' occurring by end-2027 — the brief granted no-statute-through-2028, not the occurrence of any such event; this is a second assumption riding along with the granted branch.
unresolved: Whether pressure-model's Garcia citation actually satisfies ai-courts-decide's falsifiable (i.e., whether Character Technologies/Google count as 'a frontier developer' under the claim's own terms) is not settled in the visible minutes — the objection fields are truncated before any direct rebuttal appears, so it cannot be determined whether ai-courts-decide contests the precedent's applicability or simply has not yet addressed it.
